body:
Why buildings suffer earthquake damage

During an earthquake, the ground moves and buildings respond to that movement. Their floors, walls, roofs and structural connections must resist the resulting forces and deformations.

Buildings are vulnerable when they cannot withstand or accommodate the movement imposed by shaking. Weak materials, poor connections, inadequate structural design, heavy roofs and inferior workmanship may all increase the likelihood of damage.

Earthquake risk therefore depends not only on the severity of ground shaking but also on the quality, configuration and condition of the building stock.

Common types of vulnerable buildings

Building typeImportant vulnerabilityRelevant safety principle
Unreinforced brick masonryWalls may crack, separate at corners or fail out of their plane.Provide appropriate connections and seismic-strengthening features.
Stone or earthen housesWeak bonding and heavy roofs may increase collapse risk.Improve wall integrity, wall-to-roof connections and roof safety.
Reinforced-concrete framesInadequate detailing or poor construction can cause brittle structural damage.Use appropriate seismic design and ductile detailing.
Open-ground-storey buildingsA relatively weak or flexible ground floor may concentrate earthquake deformation.Avoid abrupt weakness or provide engineered strengthening.
Buildings with unsecured componentsWater tanks, ceilings, parapets, shelves or equipment may fall.Secure vulnerable non-structural components.

Understanding the soft-storey problem

A soft storey is a storey that has significantly lower lateral stiffness than the storeys above it. This difference may cause disproportionate deformation in the more flexible storey during earthquake shaking.

In urban areas, a common example is a reinforced-concrete residential building with an open parking floor and masonry-filled floors above. The upper floors may be relatively stiff because of their infill walls, while the parking floor has fewer walls to resist lateral movement.

The open floor is not automatically unsafe merely because parking is provided. The danger arises when the change in structural stiffness or strength is not adequately addressed by seismic design and detailing.

After the 2001 Bhuj earthquake, investigations of reinforced-concrete buildings identified soft storeys, irregularities, poor detailing and deficient construction practices among the principal causes of serious damage.

Structural and non-structural vulnerability

It is important to distinguish the principal load-bearing components of a building from the components installed for use, comfort or appearance.

  • Structural components: These include columns, beams, load-bearing walls, floor systems and foundations that support the building and resist loads.
  • Non-structural components: These include cupboards, suspended ceilings, light fittings, service equipment, some partitions and other items that do not form the principal load-resisting system.

Failure of structural components may threaten the stability of a building. Failure of non-structural components can injure occupants, block exits or interrupt essential services even when the main structure remains standing.

For example, a school building may remain structurally intact while falling ceiling fixtures and unsecured shelves create serious hazards for students.

The role of local ground conditions

The same earthquake may produce different ground motion at nearby locations. The difference may result from the nature and depth of soil deposits, underlying rock and other site conditions.

Ground amplification occurs when local geological conditions increase certain components of shaking relative to other nearby locations. Deep or soft sediment deposits can sometimes produce stronger or longer-lasting shaking than nearby rock sites.

Liquefaction is another important ground-related hazard. Strong shaking of susceptible loose, saturated granular soil may cause a temporary loss of strength, leading to ground settlement or lateral movement.

Ground amplification and liquefaction must not be treated as identical processes. Amplification concerns the modification of seismic ground motion, while liquefaction concerns the loss of soil strength under suitable conditions.

Why schools, hospitals and public facilities need special attention

Some buildings are especially important because of their occupants or the services they provide. Schools contain large numbers of students, hospitals must remain available for treatment, and emergency-control facilities support public coordination.

Consequently, protecting these structures has benefits beyond the buildings themselves. Damage to a hospital can simultaneously injure occupants and reduce medical capacity when it is most needed.

Prelims focus

  • Unreinforced masonry can be vulnerable because of weak wall connections and inadequate seismic resistance.
  • A soft storey has substantially lower lateral stiffness than neighbouring storeys.
  • An open parking floor can create a soft-storey problem if it is not appropriately engineered.
  • Liquefaction involves loss of strength in susceptible saturated soil during shaking.
  • Non-structural objects can cause injuries even without collapse of the main building.
  • Trap: Reinforced-concrete construction is not automatically earthquake-resistant.

[References: Pankaj Agarwal, S. K. Thakkar and R. N. Dubey, Seismic Performance of Reinforced Concrete Buildings During Bhuj Earthquake of January 26, 2001, ISET Journal of Earthquake Technology, September 2002, pp. 195–217, abstract; IIT Kanpur, NICEE, The 2001 Bhuj Earthquake, Reinforced Concrete Buildings and field observations; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Feasibility Study on Seismic Microzonation, accessed 2 November 2026; National Disaster Management Authority, Management of Earthquakes, April 2007, Chapters 3–4.]

pictures.caption: Why a weak open ground floor can suffer concentrated earthquake damage.

title: Building Vulnerability and Local Ground Conditions in Gujarat

body:
What earthquake-resistant construction means

Earthquake-resistant construction aims to reduce the probability of structural collapse and serious injury during the earthquake effects for which a building is designed.

It does not mean that a building can never be damaged. A properly designed building may experience cracking or other damage during severe shaking while still providing much better protection against collapse.

The basic objective is to provide adequate strength, stability, continuity and capacity to undergo earthquake-induced deformation without sudden, dangerous failure.

Important principles of safer construction

  • Regular structural arrangement: Simple, reasonably regular building layouts generally avoid some of the problems caused by abrupt structural irregularities.
  • Continuous load path: Structural components need effective connections so that earthquake forces can be transferred through the building to its foundations.
  • Ductility: A suitably detailed structure can undergo deformation while retaining load-carrying capacity instead of failing suddenly in a brittle manner.
  • Appropriate roof and wall connections: Roofs, walls and structural elements should act together rather than separate dangerously during shaking.
  • Suitable construction materials and workmanship: Correct design can be undermined by weak materials, defective connections or poor construction.
  • Site-specific safety: Ground conditions and geological hazards must be considered where relevant.

These are conceptual principles for understanding earthquake safety. Actual structural design, assessment and construction decisions require qualified professionals and the applicable technical standards.

Major Indian Standards related to earthquake safety

The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) publishes technical standards used in earthquake-resistant design, construction, assessment and strengthening.

Indian StandardMain subject
IS 1893 (Part 1):2016Criteria for earthquake-resistant design and the seismic zoning framework applicable at the stated cutoff.
IS 4326:2013Earthquake-resistant design and construction of buildings.
IS 13920:2016Ductile design and detailing of reinforced-concrete structures subjected to seismic forces.
IS 13827:1993Improving earthquake resistance of earthen buildings.
IS 13828:1993Improving earthquake resistance of low-strength masonry buildings.
IS 13935:2009Seismic evaluation, repair and strengthening of masonry buildings.
IS 15988:2013Seismic evaluation and strengthening of existing reinforced-concrete buildings.

The standards address different problems. IS 13920 concerns ductile detailing of reinforced-concrete structures, whereas IS 13935 concerns evaluation, repair and strengthening of masonry buildings. IS 13827 and IS 13828 address different categories of traditionally vulnerable building construction.

Seismic-code status at the content cutoff

As of 2 November 2026, the relevant official confirmation is the Ministry of Earth Sciences statement published by the Press Information Bureau on 1 April 2026. It states that the revised seismic zonation was withdrawn in March 2026 and that the seismic zoning map under IS 1893 (Part 1):2016 remains the current standard. Therefore, the 2025 revision must not be treated as the operative zoning map merely because it was previously announced.

Building codes and legal enforcement

A technical standard and its legal enforcement are related but different matters.

BIS develops and publishes Indian Standards. The National Building Code of India 2016 provides a broader framework of building provisions, including structural safety requirements.

Building regulations, development-control rules and approval procedures bring relevant safety requirements into practical operation. The Model Building Bye-Laws 2016 contain provisions on structural safety in Chapter 6.

Urban local bodies and urban development authorities are important for building-plan approvals and enforcement of applicable building bye-laws. States and Union Territories determine their relevant regulations and inspection arrangements.

Consequently, publication of an Indian Standard does not by itself prove that every existing building complies with it. Seismic safety also requires appropriate adoption, professional design, construction supervision, inspection and enforcement.

What the 2001 earthquake taught about code compliance

The Bhuj earthquake demonstrated the consequences of inadequate implementation of seismic design principles. Some buildings suffered severe damage because their structural arrangements or construction details were insufficient for the actual shaking.

This created a strong case for improving professional training, building regulation, public awareness and the safety of both new and existing construction.

Prelims focus

  • BIS publishes Indian Standards for earthquake-resistant design and construction.
  • IS 1893 addresses earthquake-resistant structural design and seismic zoning.
  • IS 13920 addresses ductile detailing of reinforced-concrete structures.
  • IS 13827 concerns earthen buildings; IS 13828 concerns low-strength masonry.
  • The 2025 revised seismic zonation was withdrawn in March 2026; the 2016 zoning framework remains applicable at this lesson's cutoff.
  • Trap: Publication of a standard and enforcement through building regulations are not the same action.

[References: Bureau of Indian Standards, Standard Details for IS 1893 (Part 1):2016, including references to IS 4326, IS 13827, IS 13828, IS 13920, IS 13935 and IS 15988, accessed 2 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Earth Sciences, Parliament Question: Seismograph Network, 1 April 2026; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, National Framework for Structural Safety Audits and Seismic Resilience of Buildings, 23 July 2026; National Disaster Management Authority, Management of Earthquakes, April 2007, Chapter 5, pp. 24–28.]

pictures.alt: A connected building diagram shows how regular structure, load paths, connections, ductility, good construction and ground conditions reduce collapse risk.
pictures.caption: Important principles that help buildings resist earthquake damage.

title: Earthquake-Resistant Construction: Indian Standards and Enforcement

body:
What is seismic retrofitting?

Many buildings were constructed before present earthquake-safety practices were adopted or without adequate consideration of seismic forces. Such buildings may remain vulnerable even when no obvious damage is visible.

Seismic retrofitting means modifying an existing structure to improve its ability to resist earthquake effects. It is especially important where an otherwise useful building has inadequate structural resistance.

Retrofitting should be distinguished from ordinary repair and complete reconstruction.

ActionPrimary purpose
RepairRestore damaged components or their intended function.
RetrofittingImprove the existing building's performance against earthquake effects.
ReconstructionRebuild a structure that is destroyed, unsafe or otherwise unsuitable for retention.

Repair does not necessarily improve seismic resistance. For example, simply plastering over a crack may restore appearance without correcting the structural weakness responsible for the crack.

Retrofitting rural buildings

Rural settlements in Gujarat include houses made with brick, stone, earth and other locally available materials. Their earthquake performance depends on construction quality, wall connections, roof characteristics and other structural details.

In vulnerable masonry or earthen buildings, earthquake strengthening may involve:

  • Improving connections between intersecting walls.
  • Providing appropriate horizontal seismic bands to help walls act together.
  • Strengthening vulnerable corners and openings.
  • Improving connections between walls and roofs.
  • Reducing dangerous roof-related vulnerabilities where appropriate.

Horizontal bands at levels such as the lintel or roof may be important in suitable building systems. The necessary locations, materials and connections depend on the building type and its condition.

These measures must be selected and detailed with appropriate technical guidance. A strengthening method suitable for one masonry building may not be suitable for another.

Retrofitting urban buildings

Urban Gujarat contains reinforced-concrete residential, commercial and institutional buildings. Some older buildings may have irregular structural arrangements, weak ground storeys or inadequate earthquake-resistant detailing.

Depending on the findings of a professional assessment, urban seismic retrofitting may involve strengthening selected columns, adding or improving lateral-load-resisting elements, improving connections or correcting other structural weaknesses.

For buildings with open ground floors, an engineer must assess whether the ground storey possesses adequate stiffness, strength and deformation capacity. Adding structural elements without a proper assessment can create new problems by changing the behaviour of the building.

Non-structural improvements also matter. Securing overhead tanks, shelves, equipment and other potentially falling components can reduce injuries and service disruption.

How buildings should be prioritised

Not every existing building can be strengthened simultaneously. The National Disaster Management Authority recommends identifying vulnerable buildings and prioritising critical and lifeline structures.

A lifeline facility is an essential facility or infrastructure system whose functioning is important during an emergency or recovery. Examples include hospitals, emergency-control facilities, important transport links, water supply systems and electricity infrastructure.

Schools also deserve attention because they may contain large numbers of children and staff.

Priority is influenced by seismic hazard, structural vulnerability, occupancy, the consequences of failure and the importance of the facility to the community.

The general retrofitting process

Effective retrofitting begins with understanding the existing building rather than immediately carrying out construction work.

  1. Identify: Prepare an inventory of existing buildings and important facilities.
  2. Assess: Examine their structural condition, earthquake vulnerability and relevant site hazards.
  3. Prioritise: Select buildings where strengthening would reduce significant risks.
  4. Design: Have qualified professionals develop suitable strengthening measures.
  5. Implement and verify: Carry out the approved work with appropriate quality control and inspection.

Retrofitting is therefore a form of pre-disaster mitigation. It reduces possible future losses rather than waiting for a building to fail before taking corrective action.

Lessons from Gujarat's reconstruction

The rehabilitation programme after the 2001 earthquake demonstrated the importance of combining housing assistance with technical guidance and community participation.

Owner-driven reconstruction allowed affected households to participate in rebuilding their homes, while technical support helped incorporate safer construction practices.

The wider lesson is that reconstruction and retrofitting should not merely reproduce earlier vulnerabilities. The aim is to make settlements more resilient to future earthquakes.

Prelims focus

  • Seismic retrofitting improves the earthquake resistance of an existing building.
  • Repair and retrofitting are not synonymous.
  • IS 13827 and IS 13828 provide guidance relevant to earthen and low-strength masonry buildings respectively.
  • IS 13935 concerns existing masonry buildings; IS 15988 concerns existing reinforced-concrete buildings.
  • Critical and lifeline buildings receive special attention in earthquake-risk reduction.
  • Trap: Cosmetic repair of cracks does not automatically constitute seismic strengthening.

[References: National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Earthquakes, April 2007, Chapter 4, pp. 19–22, and Chapter 5, sections on rural and semi-urban construction; Bureau of Indian Standards, IS 13827:1993, IS 13828:1993, IS 13935:2009 and IS 15988:2013, standard descriptions; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Gujarat Earthquake Rehabilitation and Reconstruction Policy, introduction; World Bank, Community-Driven Disaster Recovery and Reconstruction, section on owner-driven housing construction and the Gujarat Earthquake Reconstruction Programme.]
